title: The 1971–73 Buick Riviera Makes a Bold Statement for Medium Dollars

body_markdown:
Legacies tend to last, and it’s been widely reported that GM Design VP Bill Mitchell wanted to inject some of the unforgettable style of the[1963 Corvette Sting Ray](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=D7FH299049) into the personal luxury segment. Perhaps he was onto something, as the second generation Buick Riviera did look significantly different between its first ([1966](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=1966+buick+riviera) ) and final iteration ([1970](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=1970+buick+riviera) ). That 1970 Riviera did look significantly more conservative, so Jerry Hirshberg was tasked with turning the 1971 Riviera into something akin to a luxurious Corvette Sting Ray.


While styling is always subjective, there’s little doubt that Hirshberg created something eye catching. If one wasn’t captivated by the tapered front end, its rear styling would surely seal the deal. Hirshberg did the job admirably, and certainly had a[successful career at Nissan](https://www.hagerty.com/media/design/experimental-creativity-the-early-days-of-nissan-design-international/) in the following years. While the third generation (1971–73) Riviera, nicknamed the “Boat Tail” Riviera for obvious reasons, isn’t the only reason why Nissan was courting Mr. Hirshberg, it’s likely that his successful risk taking emboldened him to create radical 1990s creations like the[Infiniti J30](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/the-infiniti-j30-was-a-super-yacht-for-the-masses/) luxury sedan.

If the Boat Tail Riv didn’t inspire confidence in one’s career in automotive design, perhaps nothing will. Because that rear deck treatment took the second generation “Mid Year” Corvette and amplified it into a bullet-shaped rear bumper on an impossibly long rear spear. Part of that extra presence came from the 1971 Riviera’s platform change to GM’s corporate B-body platform, with an extra 3 inches of wheelbase and roughly 2 inches more overall length. It also ensured easier integration with a revolutionary new traction control system, as we will discuss later.


While there was internal chatter at General Motors for the next Riviera to join the all new G-body being prepared for Pontiac’s[personal luxury Grand Prix](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/the-1969-72-pontiac-grand-prix-is-personal-luxury-and-performance-perfected/) , that smaller footprint ultimately wasn’t in the cards. It’s fun to imagine a Boat Tail Riviera with roughly 7 inches less length, 4 inches less width, and 2 inches less height, as it would take Bill Mitchell’s Sting Ray design to more assertive heights in the wildly expanding personal luxury segment.

And that segment was rapidly growing, with new arrivals like[Chevrolet’s Monte Carlo](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=1970+chevrolet+monte+carlo) ,[Dodge’s Monaco](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=dodge+monaco) , and even the enlarged[1971 Ford Mustang Grande](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ford/mustang/1971/1971-ford-mustang-grande?id=aCn1I000000DKK6SAO) (and its[Mercury Cougar](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/mercury/cougar/1971/1971-mercury-cougar-xr~7?id=aCn1I000000DPHUSA4) cousin). In a Buick press release, Lee N. Mays, Buick General Manager suggested “This classic, new design is a triumph of automotive styling, and will assure the Riviera of continuing its established reputation as the leader in the personal luxury car field.”


But that wasn’t necessarily meant to be, as Riviera sales slumped, and the 1970s ushered new requirements that wreaked havoc on its styling and performance. Although a little under 46,000 units were sold for the all-new second generation in its freshman year (1966), the market changed for the 1971 Boat Tail as under 34,000 transactions were completed. Sales for the final two years of Boat Tail Rivieras were about the same, but the growing personal luxury market rejected the fourth generation (1974) with another drop in sales volume.


While personal luxury was going mainstream, the Malaise Era’s need for less fragile bumpers ensured the Riviera had bigger bumpers with less Sting Ray swagger. It also demanded less smog, and lower compression and EGR valve integration ensured the 455 cid Buick V-8 lost power almost every year.


Buick


Vauxhall Ventora (Victor FE)


Dennis Elzinga | Wikimedia Commons


But the 1971–73 Riviera never really lost its spirit, one that is both unforgettable and likely influenced GM Vauxhall designers when creating the Victor (FE) sedan for 1972. While the 2-D photos above may not make it clear, the Victor’s grille, hood bulge, and drop away front fascia are surfaced much like the big Buick. To see it is to know it, and the Riviera-turned-Victor is also considered a[Muscle Car in India](https://madrascourier.com/insight/forever-iconic-remembering-indias-first-muscle-car-contessa/) .


Being the inspiration for other GM designs is one thing, but the Boat Tail Riviera made an impact in all the right places. And not just with its styling, but with robust V-8 thrust, impressive luxury accoutrements, and elevated technology. The latter was found in Buick’s optional MaxTrac traction control system, optional on large Buicks for 1972.


While there’s an argument that the Riviera could have looked more lithe and assertive as the downsized G-body, it’s clear that becoming a B-body ensured MaxTrac was part of the Riviera’s equation. As with its[Centurion](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/buick/centurion/1972/1972-buick-centurion-base?id=aCn1I000000DNBNSA4) cousin, the Riviera used speed sensors and a computer to “provide controlled power” in low traction situations.


MaxTrac worked by altering engine timing according to speed reports in sensors mounted in the transmission (drive wheels) and the front end (rolling wheels). While not intended solely for the Riviera, MaxTrac provided it with a strong counterpoint to Ford’s “Sure Track” rear-wheel anti-lock brake option in its[Thunderbird](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=1972+ford+thunderbird) competition. (Too bad it took decades to combine both efforts into effortless braking *and* *acceleration* on slippery surfaces!)

Buick


In many ways these big block’d, boat tailed, third gen Rivieras provided something for everyone. And maybe that’s why values are going up, while the second generation Riviera is going down. Median #3 condition (good) values for 1966 Rivieras are down 2.6% in the last three years, while a #3 condition 1971 Riviera is up 6.3%.


That translates into a median value of $18,700 for the 1966 model, and an impressive $20,200 for the 1971 model. The final model year for both generations tells a similar story, as a 1970 model rings up at $14,800 while a 1973 Riviera is an impressive $19,400. Values have also been increasing, consistently, for quite some time.


Condition #2 (excellent) values go from the low $40s to the $50K range, depending on year and trim. A big front bumper and lower horsepower ratings aren’t scaring buyers away from the final Boat Tails, and generational tastes might be a factor.


Generation X has the most quotes and policies for Boat Tails, with 41% (and 31% of the entire market). Boomers come in at 36% (34% of the market), while Millennials occupy 13% of the third generation Buick (and 20% of the market). Preboomers have 6% of this market while Gen Z is right behind at 5% (4 and 11% of the total market, respectively).

Quoted values for Boat Tails are up 6% over the last year, and other Rivieras have risen as well. A first generation 1963 model in #3 condition appreciated 11% in the last three years. Even the fourth generation (1974–76) is taking advantage of this high tide, as this boxier personal luxury coupe appreciated a stunning 28.6% in the last three years, but only to a median #3 value of $10,800.


These valuations are for base models, but the Gran Sport (GS) option adds $3600 for 1971 Rivieras, $4400 for 1966 models, but only $100 for the deep Malaise Era 1974–76 models. Stage 1 engine upgrades are generally factored into pricing for GS models, as very few examples left the factory without the GS option in tow.


To say this is uptick in Riviera values is akin to earth shattering news is certainly an exaggeration. But we are seeing a maturity in the Boat Tail Riviera’s space in the classic car space. In many ways this is Bill Mitchell’s vision coming to fruition, as maybe he was onto something when he suggested the Riviera needed to provide Sting Ray flair to the personal luxury segment.
